tagline: From Lassen to Crater Lake, volcanic rock shapes the water’s course.
intro: The Volcanic Legacy Scenic Byway links Lassen and Crater Lake through mountain forests, wetlands, farms and ranches. The Volcanic Legacy Community Partnership presents this 500-mile All-American Road as a journey through volcanic peaks, lava flows, caves, mud pots and fumaroles. At Lassen, the park road climbs to 8,512 feet; at Crater Lake, a 33-mile drive follows the caldera rim. The archived federal guide allows two days to drive the byway or five to enjoy it.

One part of this road network followed close behind an eruption. Lassen’s renewed activity began in 1914, and the surrounding national park was established in 1916. Its 29-mile Main Park Road was built between 1925 and 1931. State Route 89 runs north to south through the park, passing immediately beside the base of Lassen Peak. That road now belongs to the Lassen Scenic Byway, which is included within the California portion of Volcanic Legacy.

Begin with the Lassen and Lake Almanor loops, then head north from Old Station through Hat Creek and Burney to McCloud. Continue past Mount Shasta City and Weed, taking U.S. 97 through Butte Valley toward Dorris and Klamath Falls. Upper Klamath Lake and Fort Klamath lead toward Crater Lake; beyond the rim, the route crosses the Pumice Desert and follows Oregon 138 to U.S. 97.

moments.title: Lassen Peak
moments.text: The road passes between Lassen Peak and Bumpass Mountain, near a volcano whose 1915 eruption sent ash as far east as Elko, Nevada. The May 22 explosion was the strongest of the 1914–1917 eruptive series. Benjamin Franklin Loomis photographed the eruptions with glass-plate negatives, preparing his film and using a tent as a darkroom. A number of Loomis’s original photographic plates remain in the National Park Service archives, preserving a record of those eruptions. His pictures helped researchers understand their sequence and geology. The national park was created to preserve eruption-affected ground for study and protect nearby volcanic features.

moments.title: Burney Falls
moments.text: Burney Falls gets its water from underground as well as from the creek above it. Layered, porous basalt holds rainwater and snowmelt in a large underground reservoir, releasing it through springs at and above the 129-foot waterfall. Below the falls, Burney Creek continues into Lake Britton. Descendants of the McArthur family bought the waterfall and surrounding land to save them from development, then gave the property to the state in the 1920s. The Falls Loop Trail starts at the overlook and descends to the bottom of the falls before crossing the creek and returning.
moments.notice: Springs emerge at and above the falls, adding water to Burney Creek.

moments.title: Crater Lake
moments.text: Crater Lake occupies the basin left by Mount Mazama’s collapse, with no rivers entering or leaving it. Rain and snow replenish its water. ODOT recounts how Clarence Dutton sounded the lake from the survey boat Cleetwood using lead pipe and piano wire. The agency compares that early measurement with sonar readings taken in 1959. The landforms are visible from Rim Drive: the lake and the remnants of Mount Mazama surround a later volcanic feature, Wizard Island. Near the southern shore, the smaller Phantom Ship takes a different form: a natural pillar of rock.
moments.notice: Wizard Island is a volcanic cinder cone near the lake’s western shore.

practical: Lassen Peak: The segment of State Route 89 through Lassen Volcanic National Park is typically closed in winter because of heavy snow and snowpack. (checked 2026-10-11)
Crater Lake: ODOT lists November–May closure of the north entrance and Rim Drive, with the south entrance on Highway 62 open year-round. (checked 2026-10-11)
